spans.assertion: the analysis used data from 146,028 player-referee dyads across four European soccer leagues, 2012-2013 season
the analysis used logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors
the model adjusted for position, league country, number of games, and yellow cards
found an adjusted risk difference of 0.2052 percentage points (95% CI [-0.0259, 0.4364], p=0.0818)
the confidence interval including zero means the primary result is inconclusive
found an adjusted odds ratio of 1.187 (95% CI [0.978, 1.441], p=0.0822)
concludes the hypothesis of referee bias by skin tone is NOT SUPPORTED because the CI includes the null and p=0.082 exceeds the 0.05 threshold
states the evidence is inconclusive and does not support a definitive claim of racial bias despite a positive point estimate
reports the primary risk-difference result in full: 0.2052 pp (0.002052 probability scale), 95% CI [-0.0259, 0.4364], p=0.0818, SE=0.001179
dark-skin-toned players have an estimated 0.21 percentage point higher probability of a red card than light-skin-toned players after adjustment
interprets the CI (-0.026 to 0.44) as substantial uncertainty and, since it includes zero, an inconclusive result
reports the secondary odds-ratio result in full: 1.187, 95% CI [0.978, 1.441], p=0.0822, log-odds coefficient 0.1717 (SE 0.0988)
dark-skin-toned players have 18.7% higher odds of a red card than light-skin-toned players after adjustment
the odds-ratio CI includes 1.0, consistent with the primary analysis's inconclusive finding
defines the unit of analysis as the player-referee dyad, aggregating all encounters between a specific player and referee over their careers
found the primary analysis sample composition: N=100,135 dyads, 16,085 (16.1%) dark skin, 84,050 (83.9%) light skin, 1,243 (1.24%) red card events
found the sample includes 1,227 unique players and 2,780 unique referees
defines the outcome as binary: whether the player received at least one red card from the referee across all encounters
two independent raters coded player skin tone on a 5-point scale (0.00 very light to 1.00 very dark) from profile photos
found an inter-rater correlation of 0.924, described as excellent agreement
averaged the two raters' scores into a single skin-tone score
categorized players as Light when the average rating is ≤0.25
categorized players as Dark when the average rating is ≥0.75
defines Medium as an average rating between 0.375 and 0.625
excluded Medium skin-tone players from the primary analysis
adjusted for position group as a 5-category variable (Defender as reference; Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Other), with specified position-to-category mappings
adjusted for league country as a 4-category variable (England, France, Germany, Spain; England as reference)
adjusted for the standardized number of games in the dyad to control for exposure/opportunity
adjusted for the standardized number of yellow cards as a proxy for aggressive play style
used logistic regression with marginal effects as the model
used cluster-robust standard errors clustered by player (1,227 clusters) to account for non-independence of dyads within player
computed average marginal effects (AME) to estimate the risk difference
used Python 3.11 and statsmodels 0.14+ for the analysis
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7% of original) due to missing skin tone ratings
excluded the 17,015 Medium skin-tone dyads from the primary analysis to maximize contrast
included the Medium skin-tone dyads in a sensitivity analysis
excluded 7,471 dyads (6.9%) missing position, using complete case analysis
found the final analytic sample totals 100,135 of the original 146,028 observations (68.6%)
standardized (z-scored) the continuous covariates games and yellow cards
found the logistic regression converged successfully
found a pseudo R² of 0.072
found the likelihood ratio test shows the model is significantly better than the null (p<0.001)
concludes the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players is NOT SUPPORTED by the evidence
judges the 0.21pp adjusted risk difference as substantively small
calculates the 0.21pp difference as a 17% relative increase over the ~1.2% baseline rate for light-skinned players
states the 95% CI [-0.026, +0.44] includes zero so a null effect cannot be ruled out, and the interval is wide relative to the point estimate
states the p-value (0.082) exceeds the α=0.05 threshold, so under traditional testing they fail to reject the null
notes the point estimate is positive (consistent with the hypothesis) but the uncertainty makes a definitive conclusion untenable
states the secondary odds-ratio estimand leads to the same inconclusive conclusion as the primary estimand

concludes the data provide suggestive but inconclusive evidence of a small positive association, with the true effect potentially ranging from slightly protective to moderately harmful, insufficient to support a claim of meaningful racial bias

spans.note: Limitations and Potential Sources of Bias heading
caveats that missing skin-tone ratings (15%) and missing position (7%) could bias results if missingness is non-random
caveats about subjectivity of skin-tone coding, information loss from binary categorization, and photo-quality effects
caveats about lacking data on player behavior, reputation, match-level factors, referee characteristics, and yellow cards being an imperfect proxy
caveats that dyad-level aggregation obscures within-match variation and rare red-card events reduce power

spans.assertion: did not cluster standard errors by referee, only by player, which may underestimate SEs if referee effects matter

spans.note: caveat that single-season data may not generalize to other periods
caveat that the observational design cannot establish causality; association could reflect referee bias, player behavior differences, residual confounding, or interaction effects
caveats that results may not generalize beyond European leagues or to women's soccer

spans.assertion: states the primary analysis was pre-specified
states the exploratory subgroup analyses by position and country are vulnerable to Type I error if over-interpreted

ran a sensitivity analysis re-including the Medium skin-tone category (N=116,160), finding Dark-vs-Light risk difference of 0.2091pp (95% CI [-0.0222,0.4404], p=0.076) and Medium-vs-Light of 0.1713pp (95% CI [-0.0460,0.3887], p=0.122)
concludes results are robust to including medium-toned players, with both dark and medium groups showing small, non-significant positive associations versus light
found an unadjusted risk difference of 0.195pp with a chi-square test p=0.045 (significant at α=0.05)
concludes the unadjusted significant difference diminishes to non-significance after adjustment, suggesting confounding by position, league, and play style
found unadjusted position-subgroup differences: Midfielder +0.22pp, Forward +0.28pp, Other +0.35pp, Defender +0.07pp, Goalkeeper +0.06pp
found unadjusted league-subgroup differences: Germany +0.68pp, England +0.42pp, France -0.61pp, Spain -0.32pp
notes effects vary by position/league suggesting heterogeneity, but interaction tests were non-significant (p=0.46 for position) and subgroup analyses are underpowered
assumed log-linear relationships on the logit scale
judges the linearity assumption as reasonably met given categorical predictors
assesses the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption as LIKELY VIOLATED due to lack of data on player behavior, reputation, and match context
assesses correct model specification as reasonable based on interaction tests, though heterogeneity exists
assesses the independent-clusters assumption as reasonably met
assesses the missing-data-mechanism assumption (MCAR/MAR) as UNCERTAIN and not fully verifiable
identifies unmeasured confounding as the most critical concern, with the direction of potential bias unclear
lists strengths: large sample size (>100,000 dyads), high-quality independent-rater skin-tone coding, cluster-robust inference for player dependence, and adjustment for key confounders
asserts that the rarity of red cards reduces false-positive risk due to bias amplification

spans.note: forward-looking recommendations not carried out in this analysis: match-level analysis, video coding, referee fixed effects, experimental designs, replication

spans.assertion: reports excellent inter-rater reliability (r=0.92), no obvious data entry errors, and reasonable variable distributions
asserts all analyses are fully reproducible from the submitted script (final_analysis.py) and dataset (soccer.csv)
states the script includes complete data preprocessing, model specification/estimation, computation of all reported statistics, and sensitivity analyses
used Python 3.11, pandas 2.0+, numpy 1.24+, statsmodels 0.14+, scipy 1.10+

spans.note: dataset provenance (European leagues, 2012-2013, N=146,028 dyads, 2,053 players, 3,147 referees); player/referee counts here are for the full original dataset, differing from the 1,227/2,780 figures given for the analytic subsample

spans.assertion: states the two skin-tone raters coded blind
